units.spoken: Deep Q-Networks (DQN)
Learn from readings that never repeat, without chasing your own guesses.
Some worlds never show the same situation twice, so a list of move values, one per situation, can never be filled. What can stand in for that list, and how do you keep it steady while it learns?

Here the agent is the banana collector, which senses the arena through sensor readings, real numbers that change a little with every step. The arena holds yellow and blue bananas; the collector is paid for each yellow it eats and charged for each blue, until time runs out.

Take a look at this figure. The arena is a world where the collector never stands in the same place twice, so no list of situations could ever cover it. The readings shift a little with every step, which is why a table of scores cannot work here. The collector has to learn a rule that turns fresh readings into a move, not a lookup. That gap, between a world that never repeats and a learner that must still act well, is the problem this tutorial solves.

Figure 1 looks down on the arena, with the collector as the blue dot and rays reaching out from it. Take a ray that hits a yellow banana close by: the reading says a yellow banana is near, so the collector turns toward it.

The agent is the learner that picks the moves, as taught in RL Basics. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad, as taught in RL Basics. An episode is one run from the start until it ends, as taught in RL Basics. Each new episode drops fresh bananas around the arena.
Section one, The banana arena
The collector senses a list of real-valued readings and has a short list of moves.

The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less, as taught in RL Basics. A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance, as taught in RL Basics. Yellows and blues lie mixed together, so the way to a yellow can pass close to a blue.

A move's value, also called its score, is the return the agent expects if it makes move a in state s and plays on from there, as taught in RL Basics. A Q-table keeps one score for every state and move, as taught in Q-Learning. The collector's readings almost never repeat, so it almost never meets the same state twice.

Epsilon-greedy usually plays the top-scored move and, with chance epsilon, a random one instead, as taught in RL Basics. The exploring chance shrinks after each episode. Early in training most of its steps are random, so it sees much of the arena before it trusts its scores.

What this figure is teaching is that a network can stand in for the table. The readings go in and one score per move comes out, so the collector never needs to have seen a spot before to score it. Spots with nearly the same readings get nearly the same scores, which means what the collector learns in one corner carries to the next. The network is not a lookup; it is a rule that generalises, and that rule is what DQN trains.

Figure 2 shows how the collector turns its readings into move scores, with one network doing the whole job. The readings go in on the left, the network in the middle mixes them through its layers, and one score per move comes out on the right, the top score naming the move the collector plays. Take readings from a spot near a yellow banana: the score for the move toward it comes out highest, so the collector turns that way.
This code runs one episode, picking moves epsilon-greedy.
1. eps is the exploring chance.
2. A fresh episode, with fresh bananas, runs until the episode ends.
3. agent holds the network and the past steps in one object. Each move stores its step, and the agent learns from the stored steps later, once enough are stored.
4. After the episode, eps shrinks, so random moves get rarer.

sections.section: 2 From a Q-table to a network

units.spoken: Section two, From a Q-table to a network
A network stands in for the table

Picture the collector's readings as a list of numbers that changes a little with every step, so no table could hold a score for every list. Function approximation means a network takes that list in and gives back one score per move. Lists that look nearly alike get nearly alike scores, so what is learned in one spot carries to the next.
How. The readings go in, the weights mix them through the layers, and one score per move comes out.
When it works, a spot the collector has never stood in still gets a sensible score.
The features are the numbers a network reads about a state. In the arena two spots with almost the same readings now share one learned score, and a spot never seen before still gets a sensible guess.

The discount is a number under one that shrinks the reward of each later step by one more power, as taught in RL Basics. Q-learning's target is the step's reward plus the discounted best move value in the next state, as taught in Q-Learning. So the collector can learn from a single step, without waiting for time to run out.
A network that outputs one score per move is a Q-network, and training it with Q-learning's target is a Deep Q-Network, DQN for short.
2.1 Learning from old steps, off-policy

Best play is the policy that earns the most return; Q star is each move's value under it, as taught in RL Basics. Off-policy means learning the values of one policy while playing another, as taught in SARSA. So steps taken long ago by an older, more random policy are still fair training data for Q-learning's target.
2.2 Replay memory reuses past steps
Learn from old steps, shuffled

Picture the memory as a long row of past steps, oldest on the left and newest on the right. Steps that follow each other look almost the same, so training on them in a row teaches the same lesson many times.
How. Every step joins the row, and each training step draws a batch, a handful from it at random, scattered across the whole row.
When it works, one batch mixes the collector's early wandering with its later runs, so each batch teaches something fresh.
Replay memory, the replay buffer in the code, comes from an early method that reused past steps instead of learning from each step once and throwing it away.

Here is the point of this figure. A batch drawn at random from the whole memory mixes the collector's early wandering with its later runs, so each batch teaches something fresh. Steps that follow each other look almost the same, so training on them in a row would teach the same lesson many times. Scattering the batch across the memory breaks that repetition, and that is why random batches learn faster than recent ones.

Figure 3 shows the replay memory as a row of past steps, with one random batch ringed inside it. The ringed steps are scattered across the memory instead of taken in a row. Take the ringed batch: its steps come from far-apart moments, spread across the whole row.
2.3 A slow copy for the targets
A slow copy holds the targets still
Picture two networks side by side: the live one that learns, and a slow copy that only hands out targets. If the live one also set the targets, each update would move the target it chases.

How. The live network learns from the batch while the slow copy reads the targets. After every update the slow copy takes a tiny share of the live weights and keeps almost all of its own: that small step is the soft update. A hard copy would overwrite it outright instead.
When it works, the targets hold still from one batch to the next, and the live scores climb toward them.
The live network is the Q-network being trained, with weights phi. The target network is a slow copy of the Q-network, with weights phi prime, that computes the targets.

In the equations below, an arrow means replace the left side with the right side. The original DQN method copies the live weights outright every so often; my Value-based-methods repo on GitHub blends a little after every update.

Take a look at this figure. The training loop is a circle that never stops: act and remember, learn from a random batch, let the slow copy creep after the live network, and explore a little less each episode. Each part feeds the next, so the scores climb while the targets hold still. The loop is the whole method in one picture, and every piece of it matters: break any one part and the learning wobbles.

Figure 4 shows the training loop as four boxes, each one feeding the next around the loop. The collector acts and remembers every step, learns from random past steps every few steps, the slow copy follows the live network a little after every learning step, and random moves get rarer each episode. Take one pass round the loop: the collector moves, the step joins the memory, a batch trains the network, and the slow copy creeps after it.

sections.section: 3 A training step with replay and a slow copy

units.spoken: Section three, A training step with replay and a slow copy
One training step from memory
Picture one training step as a round trip: a handful of remembered steps, a batch, is drawn from memory, each one is scored against a target, and the scores are nudged toward their targets.

How. The slow copy sets each target, the live network gives its score for the move actually played, and the gap between them is the surprise. The loss averages the per-step error costs over the batch, and one gradient step shrinks it.
When it works, each batch pulls the live scores closer to their targets, and the collector eats more yellow than blue as training goes on.
The TD (temporal difference) error is how much one step surprised the agent, the target minus the current guess, as taught in RL Basics.
The learning rate sets how big a step each update takes.

Equation 1. The collector's readings are different on nearly every step, so a network with weights phi stands in for the table, and each training step learns from a batch of remembered steps. A delivery robot in a warehouse senses its warehouse through readings that never repeat and needs the same step: learn from remembered runs, not from a table.
Take a look at this equation. It learns from a batch of remembered steps.

The target line. Y sub i is the target for one remembered step. R sub i is the step's reward, the banana eaten. Gamma is the discount, so the next score counts almost in full. One minus done drops the next score on the last step. The slow copy's score is Q of s prime and a prime. The max takes the largest score over the moves in the next state, not the played move. The semicolon means computed with the slow copy's weights. Intuitively, the target is the reward now plus the discounted best score from the next state.
termList: Q of s prime and a prime

units.spoken: Intuition. A target is the value a live score is pulled toward.
Example. Take a remembered step where the collector eats a yellow banana and lands facing another one. The target adds the banana eaten to the slow copy's best score from the new spot.

The surprise line. Delta sub i is the surprise in one remembered step. Y sub i is the target, built from the slow copy. Q of s sub i and a sub i is the score. The minus reads as a gap. A positive gap means the step turned out better than guessed, so its score should rise. A negative gap means worse, so it should fall. A zero gap means the guess was exactly right. The semicolon means computed with the live weights. Intuitively, the surprise is the gap between what a step earned and what the live network guessed.
termList: Q of s sub i and a sub i

units.spoken: Intuition. A wide gap means the guess was far off.
Example. Take a remembered step whose live score sits below its target. The gap is positive, so the loss pulls that score up toward the target.

The loss line. L of phi is the loss, one number for the whole batch. One over B divides by the batch size. ell of delta sub i is the error cost for one step. The sum over i adds the error cost for each step in the batch. Change phi and every score, every surprise, and the loss all change. One gradient step on this loss moves the live weights to shrink it. Intuitively, the loss rolls the whole batch's surprises into one number to shrink.
Intuition. One step's surprise is not enough to train on.
Example. Take a batch of remembered steps with one wild surprise among mostly small ones. The loss averages their error costs, so the wild one's squared error cost pulls the step hard.

The penalty line. ell of delta is the penalty for one step's error. One half keeps the penalty gentle for small errors. Squaring means doubling the surprise quadruples the penalty. Intuitively, squaring punishes big errors far more than small ones.
Intuition. A penalty should punish big errors more than small ones.
Example. Take a step whose surprise is small. Its penalty is half the surprise squared, so a small error costs little.

The soft update line. Phi prime on the left is the slow copy's weights. Tau is the soft-update share, a tiny share. Phi is the live weights the slow copy takes from. One minus tau is the share kept from the slow copy. The arrow reads replace with. The shares add to one, so the slow copy's new weights are a weighted average. Intuitively, the slow copy creeps forward a little each update.
Intuition. The slow copy must follow the live network, but slowly, or the target chases itself.
Example. Take the slow copy after one update. It holds almost all of its old weights and only a tiny share of the live ones, so the next batch aims at nearly the same target.
The update this card spells out is Q-learning's, as taught in Q-Learning.

sections.section: 4 A DQN update, step by step

units.spoken: Section four, A DQN update, step by step

What this figure is teaching is that one training step is a round trip through six stages, and each stage lights only the parts it uses. The target is built first, from the slow copy, before any score moves. Then the live network's score is compared against it, the loss averages the surprises, and the slow copy creeps forward. Watching which parts stay lit at each stage shows how the pieces fit together.

Try stepping through the six stages with the Next button. Watch which parts stay lit at each stage: only the parts that stage uses. The target is built first, from the slow copy, before any score moves, and the slow copy creeps forward last.

Figure 5 walks one training step through six stages, the diagram and the card lighting together. Stage 1 lights the world, memory and live network; stage 2 lights only the memory, where a batch is drawn at random from far-apart moments. Stage 3 lights the target network and the target with line 1; stage 4 adds the live network, the played value and the gap with line 2; stage 5 lights the loss with lines 3 and 4; stage 6 lights the soft update with line 5. Take stage 4: the live network and the target sit lit together, and the gap between them is the surprise.

A plain Q-network.

sections.section: 6 Why random batches from memory matter

units.spoken: Section six, Why random batches from memory matter

Here the agent is a warehouse robot that must reach its charging dock. The floor is a grid of cells, one per place the robot can stand. The ledge is the strip of floor between the start and the dock. It starts in one bottom corner and the dock sits in the other.

Each move's reward is minus the battery it uses, so the best total is the one closest to zero. Every move costs a little battery; stepping onto the ledge costs a lot and puts the robot back at the start; only reaching the dock ends the episode. The cheapest way to the dock is the shortest path that never steps onto the ledge.
Here the features say which cells are near the robot's cell. A small network learns the floor, so its estimate of the best move value on the ringed square can be checked against the true best value.
Random batches settle on the true value, while recent-step batches with a large step blow the estimate up.

Here is the point of this figure. The batch and the step size together decide whether the robot's estimate settles or blows up. Random batches mix far-apart moments, so the estimate climbs steadily toward best play. Recent-step batches feed the network the same lesson over and over, and with a large step that repetition blows the estimate up. The tool lets you feel that difference by trying both.

Try the two batch choices and the two step sizes. With random memory, watch the estimate climb toward best play. Switch to recent steps with a large step and watch it blow up instead. The batch and the step size together decide whether the estimate settles.

Figure 6 shows a warehouse robot learning its floor from batches of remembered steps, with the batch and step size under the reader's control. The top row picks the batch, recent steps or random memory, and the step size, small and steady or large and fast, while the floor shows the batch in orange and the chart tracks the best move value on the ringed square against best play. Take the run at rest: random memory with a large step size, and the purple line is still on its way to best play.

sections.section: 7 Learning every few steps from a growing memory

units.spoken: Section seven, Learning every few steps from a growing memory
7.1 How often the agent acts and learns
The agent acts every step. It learns every few steps, once memory holds a batch, and the target moves with every learning step.
7.2 The settings my repo ran with
CleanRL offers single-file RL examples. Stable-Baselines3 is a widely used RL library. Udacity set the banana task and its solve bar.
This table is my repo's settings. Find a setting in the first column and read across for the value my repo used and what raising or lowering it does.
Take the batch size row: it sets how many remembered steps each training step learns from at once.
My repo's agent also includes the two refinements named in Section 10: Double DQN and Dueling DQN.
7.3 My run's learning curve

Take a look at this figure. The run's average climbs toward the solve bar and levels off there, which is what learning looks like when it works. The band holds the single episodes, so its width shows how much the run still varies from one episode to the next. The line is the running average, the steady signal underneath that noise. Reaching the bar and staying there is the run's proof that the agent learned.

Figure 7 shows my agent's run as it learns, episode by episode, against the bar it had to reach. The pale band holds the single episodes, the line is their running average over recent episodes, and the dashed solve bar is the average total the run had to reach. Take the end of the run: the running average levels off at the 13 solve bar, while the band holds steady around it.
7.4 The trained agent at work

What this figure is teaching is that the trained agent's scores now tell yellow from blue. It heads for the yellow bananas and curves around the blue ones, which is exactly what the rewards taught it. The clip is the payoff for the whole tutorial: the network that once guessed at random now reads fresh readings and picks the move that pays. That is what a trained DQN looks like at work.

Figure 8 shows the trained agent at work in the arena, after the learning in the earlier figures. Take one pass in the clip: the view moves through the arena past yellow and blue bananas, the two kinds its scores now tell apart.

sections.section: 8 When a network beats a table

units.spoken: Section eight, When a network beats a table
DQN fits when the states are too many or too varied for a table, and the moves come as a short list. When the states fit in a table, plain Q-Learning is simpler and steadier.
Section nine, What makes DQN unstable
This table lists what makes DQN unstable. Find a cause in the first column and read across for the symptom and the fix.
Take the missing done mask row: the scores climb past any return the agent really earns, and the fix drops the next-state term on the last step.

sections.section: 10 Refining move scores, and moves that are amounts

units.spoken: Section ten, Refining move scores, and moves that are amounts
10.1 Refining how move scores are computed
Double DQN: the live network picks
Picture the slow copy's best score as a lucky guess: among scores that are still guesses, the biggest one is usually the one that guessed too high, so the targets run high.

How. The live network picks the move that looks best in the next state, the best move, and the slow copy scores only that move, Q of s prime and a star, with weights phi prime, so a lucky guess in the live network is scored by the slow copy instead of by itself.
When it works, the targets stop running high and the scores settle near the returns the collector really earns.
Dueling DQN splits spot from move

Picture each move score as two parts added together: how good the spot itself is, and how much this move adds over the rest. Where every move is much the same, learning the spot's worth once teaches all its moves at once.

How. The network outputs the spot's worth V of s and one extra number per move, A of s and a, and each move score is the spot's worth plus its extra number minus the average extra over all moves. The extras stay centred: they average to zero because the mean is subtracted.
When it works, spots the collector visits often get their worth right sooner, and the move scores follow.
Each move score still comes out as one number, and the target's max reads them as they are.
10.2 When a move is an amount
A move that is an amount, like how hard a motor pushes, needs a different method. Continuous-Action RL handles moves that are amounts.

DQN learns move values and picks the best one. The other big family learns the policy directly, nudging it toward moves that paid off. That family is Policy Gradients, later in the series. The next page is Double DQN.
